title: Can you use AI-generated videos commercially? Rights checklist
summary: Yes, when your AI tool plan and every source asset permit it. Check music, stock, likeness, disclosure and copyright before using an AI video in ads or client work.
body_markdown:
## Quick answer


**Yes, AI-generated video can be used commercially when your tool plan permits it and you have rights to every input.**


Check music, stock footage, logos, people, voices, and client assets separately. A paid generation plan does not clear those rights or guarantee copyright protection in a fully AI-generated output. Save the terms and permissions that applied when you made the video.


This is a practical US-oriented clearance guide, checked against current primary sources on September 23, 2026. Laws, platform rules, and tool terms vary by jurisdiction and change over time. For a high-stakes campaign or disputed rights, get advice on the exact assets and markets involved.


## The four questions to answer before publishing


**1. Does the generation service allow commercial use on this plan?** Read the live plan terms for the account and generation route you actually used. A free guest output, paid subscription, API output, and third-party model hosted in another app may have different permissions. Save the dated terms or checkout screen; do not infer a license from the absence of a watermark.


**2. Can you use the inputs for this purpose?** Check every uploaded image, source video, piece of music, script, font, stock asset, logo, and reference. A license to display stock footage in a finished ad may not allow uploading it for AI transformation or creating derivatives. Confirm the specific permitted use, geography, duration, media, and client before production.


**3. Are identifiable people and brands cleared?** A synthetic likeness, cloned voice, recognizable uniform, product mark, or implied endorsement can create separate publicity, privacy, trademark, contract, or advertising issues. Obtain the performer or rights-holder permission your use requires. A model-generated face is not a substitute for that check when it resembles a real person.


**4. Does the finished video meet destination rules?** Review the ad network, publisher, client, and platform policies where it will run. A video can be allowed by a generator but rejected by a distribution platform. Check disclosure settings, factual claims, music identification, sponsorship labels, and any regulated-category rules before the final export.


## Magic Hour commercial use: what the current pages say


Magic Hour’s current[AI Video Generator product page](https://magichour.ai/products/ai-video-generator) says subscriptions and credit-pack purchases permit commercial use of outputs, while users without either purchase are limited to personal, non-commercial use. Its FAQ repeats that paid subscriptions and credit packs permit commercial use. Check the live page and your account status when you generate; a free trial or no-sign-up run is not a commercial license by itself.


The[Magic Hour Terms of Service](https://magichour.ai/terms-of-service) say you own assets you create with the service, subject to the Terms. They also require lawful inputs and prohibit infringement, impersonation, and misleading activity. That contract allocation is distinct from whether copyright law protects a particular output or whether you obtained rights to third-party inputs.


For a clean commercial trial, use[Magic Hour’s AI Video Generator](https://magichour.ai/products/ai-video-generator) with an original prompt or a brand-owned image, keep the plan record, and review the output before placing it in an ad. If the project also needs a voice, performer, logo, or music, clear those elements separately.


## Three examples: what changes the answer


### 1. Product ad from your own packshot


A shop owns the product photo, brand mark, and script, uses a commercial-eligible generation plan, and creates a ten-second product animation. The remaining checks are practical: are the claims accurate, does the generated product match the actual item, is the soundtrack owned or licensed for paid media, and do platform ad rules permit the final creative? Keep the original packshot, plan terms, music license, approval, and exported ad together.


If the packshot came from a supplier or marketplace, verify the license rather than assuming that a seller may transform it. If the model changes the product’s material, features, label, or performance, correct the video or remove the claim before publishing.


### 2. Client avatar with a cloned voice


An agency may have a commercial tool plan but still need a performer agreement covering the use of the person’s image and voice, synthetic reproduction, campaign channels, term, territories, edits, and client handoff. The approved script must not imply statements the person never authorized. Keep the signed permission and the approved final take, not just the AI output file.


Do not treat a generic consent to appear in a filmed ad as consent to create a reusable digital double. If the performer, client, or platform has additional restrictions, those controls govern the project even when the generator permits commercial output.


### 3. Social video built from stock and generated transitions


A brand licenses stock footage, adds generated transition shots, and posts the result as a sponsored video. The stock license must cover the intended channel and any AI transformation; the music needs its own rights; the sponsorship and realistic synthetic elements may need disclosure. Save the specific stock license, edit history, and platform settings alongside the final export.


If the license forbids model training or transformation, use the footage only in a permitted edit or choose another source. The generated transitions do not cleanse rights problems in the original clips.


## Commercial permission is different from copyright ownership


A service can contractually permit you to sell, publish, or advertise with its output without promising that every frame is copyrightable. The US Copyright Office’s[AI copyrightability report](https://www.copyright.gov/ai/Copyright-and-Artificial-Intelligence-Part-2-Copyrightability-Report.pdf) says purely AI-generated material, or material without enough human control over expressive elements, is not protected by US copyright. Human-authored expression, creative arrangement, and creative modification can be protected; the analysis is case-specific. Prompts alone generally do not provide sufficient control under the Office’s current analysis.


For a client deliverable, document what humans contributed: original script, storyboard, source photography, shot selection, compositing, edits, music choices, and final arrangement. This record does not create rights that do not exist, but it helps separate your own creative work from generated material and third-party assets. Review the[Copyright Office AI initiative](https://www.copyright.gov/ai/) for updated guidance.


## Disclosure, endorsements, and realistic synthetic media


A realistic AI clip can mislead even when every source file is licensed. The[FTC’s endorsement guidance](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/advertising-marketing/endorsements-influencers-reviews) addresses truthful endorsements and material connections. Do not fabricate a customer testimonial or imply that a real person used or endorsed a product when they did not. Disclose sponsorships and other material relationships as required for the placement.


YouTube’s[altered or synthetic content guidance](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/14328491?hl=en-au) requires creators to disclose realistic content that is meaningfully altered or generated, including a real person appearing to say something they did not say or a realistic scene that did not occur. Minor edits and clearly unrealistic scenes are treated differently. Check the current upload flow for the exact setting; other platforms have their own rules.


A label is useful context, not a permission slip. It does not authorize a person’s likeness, an unlicensed song, or a false performance claim. When a viewer might mistake an AI scene for documentary footage, add clear context in the creative as well as the platform’s disclosure control.


## A six-step rights check you can reuse


**Define the use.** Write the client, product, audience, countries, channels, paid-versus-organic distribution, term, and whether the video can be edited or reused. Broad terms such as “social” can hide a paid-ad restriction.


**Record the service permission.** Save the generator, plan, model or tool route, date, and live commercial-use terms. If several services touch the asset, check each one. A paid plan from the final editor does not override a restriction on an upstream generator.


**Inventory each source.** For every image, clip, sound, font, logo, script, and reference, note its owner, license or consent document, permitted transformations, and expiry. Replace uncertain assets before generation rather than trying to clear them after the creative is approved.


**Check people and claims.** Review performers, voices, public figures, testimonials, product details, health or financial claims, and brand marks. Stop any synthetic endorsement that is not authorized or any generated visual that makes the real product look materially different.


**Review the complete export.** Watch at delivery size with sound. Look for accidental logos, recognizable faces, copied-looking scenes, incorrect text, unlicensed audio, and changes in the product or offer. A thumbnail or first frame is not a sufficient review.


**Archive the approval.** Keep the final file, sources, dated terms, licenses, releases, script, disclosures, and sign-off together. Recheck when you change the placement, market, talent, music, or client; an old approval may not cover the new use.


### Make a commercial-ready first draft


Start with your own prompt or approved media. Before publishing, apply the rights check above to every input and the final export.

## What to do when a right is unclear


Do not publish on a guess. Ask the asset owner or provider for the exact permitted use in writing, replace the uncertain material, or narrow the campaign to what is clearly licensed. For a client campaign, record the open question and assign one person to resolve it before sign-off. This is usually cheaper than rebuilding a launched ad.


For choosing a tool rather than clearing a specific deliverable, compare[AI video tools for commercial use](https://magichour.ai/blog/best-ai-video-tools-for-commercial-use) . For broader generation capabilities, see[the AI video generator guide](https://magichour.ai/blog/best-ai-video-generators) . This page answers the separate question of whether a particular finished video is ready for commercial distribution.

## Frequently asked questions


###


Potentially, if your creation tool permits commercial use, every source asset is cleared, and the video follows YouTube’s monetization and synthetic-content rules. Monetization eligibility and copyright ownership are separate questions.


###


No. A paid generation plan governs the service’s output layer. Obtain the rights required for each uploaded or included song, stock asset, brand, voice, and person.


###


The current Magic Hour AI Video Generator page says users without a subscription or credit-pack purchase are limited to personal, non-commercial use. Check the live plan terms before running a campaign.


###


In the United States, the Copyright Office says purely AI-generated material is not protected, while human-authored expression or sufficiently creative arrangement or modification may be. Each work needs its own analysis.


###


Do not imply a real person endorses or says something without appropriate authorization. Likeness, voice, endorsement, contract, and platform rules may apply independently of the generator’s terms.
